frictions.title: Inaccessible availability grid cells
frictions.description: The interactive grid cells for selecting availability and viewing group availability are implemented as empty divs without ARIA roles, accessible names, or keyboard focusability. VoiceOver reads the visual time and date labels but completely bypasses the operable cells, and pressing Tab skips the entire grid, making it impossible to input or read availability nonvisually.

interventions.description: Make the availability grid cells focusable, identifiable, and operable for screen readers.

The availability grid cells (used to select personal availability and view group availability) are implemented as empty divs without ARIA roles, accessible names, or keyboard focusability. VoiceOver reads the surrounding time and date labels but never encounters the interactive cells, and Tab skips the entire grid. The user attempted to activate cells with VO-Space and the Spacebar but nothing happened, and they eventually abandoned the scheduling task because they could not input or read availability nonvisually.
interventions.mitigation: Make each grid cell a focusable interactive control. For personal availability cells, add a semantic role (e.g., button), an accessible name derived from the cell's date and time, and keyboard handling so Enter and Space trigger the same toggle action as a pointer click. For group availability cells, provide an accessible role and name, and ensure the availability tooltip is also shown on keyboard focus. Dynamically update the accessible state/label when availability changes so screen-reader users receive current status.

frictions.title: Fragmented reading of inline links
frictions.description: VoiceOver reads a single instructional sentence in five separate fragments because it stops individually on the text nodes and inline links, requiring extra navigation steps to read the complete thought.

interventions.description: The instructional sentence contains inline links that VoiceOver treats as separate accessibility stops. When the user navigates sequentially, they hear the text in five fragments (text nodes and links individually) instead of as one coherent sentence. This forces extra navigation steps and makes the instruction harder to follow, especially for screen-reader users who read by element.
interventions.mitigation: Present the instruction as a single static text unit while keeping the links separately operable. For example, place the full sentence in one text element and move links outside the sentence flow, or use an ARIA grouping technique (such as role="text") so assistive technologies announce the sentence as one unit without removing the links.

frictions.title: Inaccessible custom availability grid
frictions.description: The interactive availability grid is built with generic div elements lacking table or grid semantics. As the user navigates sequentially, VoiceOver reads the time labels but announces the adjacent grid rows generically as "group". The actual time slots are empty elements without accessible names, roles, or states, preventing nonvisual users from perceiving or toggling their availability.

interventions.description: Implement ARIA grid semantics and keyboard navigation for the availability grid.

The availability grid is built from generic div elements with no grid/row/gridcell roles, accessible names, focusability, or state information. VoiceOver announces time labels followed by generic "group", and the user cannot perceive individual time slots or toggle their availability. The core scheduling interaction is therefore inaccessible to screen reader and keyboard-only users.
interventions.mitigation: Add ARIA grid semantics: role="grid" on the slots container, role="row" on row containers, and role="gridcell" with tabindex="-1" and an accessible label on each slot cell. Implement a roving tabindex with arrow-key navigation, and handle Space/Enter to trigger the existing click-to-toggle behavior, updating each cell's accessible name and state after selection.

frictions.title: Missing page landmarks
frictions.description: The user opened the VoiceOver Landmarks rotor menu to navigate the page structure but found no items. The page lacks ARIA landmarks or HTML5 sectioning elements, preventing quick structural navigation.

interventions.description: Add ARIA landmarks to the main page sections to enable structural navigation.

The page exposes no ARIA landmarks or equivalent semantic regions, so the VoiceOver Landmarks rotor is empty. A screen reader user cannot jump directly to the main scheduling content and must move sequentially through the entire page, significantly increasing navigation effort and making it harder to build a mental model of the page structure.
interventions.mitigation: Add landmark roles to the page's top-level sections: for example, role="banner" on the menu container, role="main" on the main content container, and role="contentinfo" on the footer. This will make the page structure available through the Landmarks rotor and allow screen reader users to bypass repeated content.

frictions.title: Unlabeled utility frame in rotor
frictions.description: The VoiceOver Frames rotor lists an item generically as 'frame 1'. The lack of a descriptive title attribute prevents the user from understanding the frame's purpose without navigating into it.

interventions.description: Hide utility iframes from screen readers to reduce rotor clutter.

Utility iframes appear in the VoiceOver Frames rotor with the generic label "frame 1" and no descriptive title. The user cannot tell what a frame contains without entering it, and these frames add noise to structural navigation, making it harder to locate meaningful content.
interventions.mitigation: Hide non-essential utility iframes from assistive technology by adding aria-hidden="true" and tabindex="-1". For any frame that remains exposed, provide a descriptive title attribute so screen reader users can understand its purpose without entering it.

items.pathway_description: Skip-to-content then manual VO cursor movement to the category row; items one by one are unintelligible.

frictions.description: Product-category links are all announced as 'Visit linked content', so the user cannot determine which category each link opens.

items.description: Give each product-category link a distinct accessible name that identifies its destination category.

frictions.title: "Add to Cart" buttons lack product context
frictions.description: The "Add to Cart" buttons for each product are labeled generically. When navigating by buttons or out of context, a screen reader user cannot determine which product will be added to their cart without exploring surrounding elements.

interventions.description: Append the product name to the accessible name of each 'Add to Cart' button.

Multiple 'Add to Cart' buttons on the Shop page use identical text and have no programmatic association with their corresponding product names. A VoiceOver user navigating by buttons or form controls hears 'Add to Cart' repeatedly and cannot determine which product the button refers to without exploring surrounding content. This makes it difficult and error-prone to add a specific item to the cart, especially for users who navigate by control list rather than by page order.
interventions.mitigation: Enhance the accessible name of each 'Add to Cart' button so it includes the product name. For each .sqs-add-to-cart-button, identify the associated product list item and extract its product title, then set the button's aria-label to 'Add to Cart: [Product Title]'. Alternatively, include the product title as visually hidden text inside the button so the accessible name is generated from the button contents.

frictions.title: Carousel buttons have generic names
frictions.description: The buttons in the content carousel are all announced generically as 'Visit linked content, button' by VoiceOver, failing to convey which specific category (Characters, Watch, Read, etc.) each button leads to.

interventions.description: Replace the generic 'Visit linked content' label on carousel buttons with descriptive names based on their associated images.

The carousel buttons are announced by VoiceOver as 'Visit linked content, button', which is identical for every item. A screen reader user cannot tell from the button label whether it leads to Characters, Watch, Read, or another category. The user must inspect surrounding content or traverse several items before finding the intended destination, increasing navigation effort and risking activation of the wrong item.
interventions.mitigation: Provide a descriptive accessible name for each carousel button that reflects the specific category or destination it links to. Derive the name from the associated image's alt text or a hidden descriptive label and apply it via aria-label (e.g., 'Visit Little Leaders Characters'). Ensure the accessible name is unique and informative for each button.

The only caveat is the script's self-check notes zero matching buttons in the final /shop snapshot, but the carousel friction was observed on the homepage where the repair applies.
judge.report_note: GAM produced a developer-facing report item for the matched friction with a concrete mitigation: use descriptive accessible names derived from associated image alt text or hidden labels so screen reader users can distinguish the category links.
judge.pattern_note: Inferred interaction patterns include VoiceOver sequential navigation and keyboard focus navigation, and the recording name includes 'blind', clearly establishing the nonvisual VoiceOver context.

blind.description: The Elfsight photo-gallery carousel exposes each slide as a generic `div role="button" aria-label="Visit linked content"` (repeated many times because Swiper duplicates slides), so a screen-reader user hears a dozen identical, purpose-less controls with no idea of the destination.

The Elfsight previous/next controls are `div role="button" aria-label="Previous"/"Next"` with no `tabindex`, so they are not focusable and a keyboard/screen-reader user cannot move through that gallery at all.

Both the desktop and mobile header markup (plus the overlay menu) are present in the DOM, so the Shop/Books/Playground/About links, the "Login" link and the "0 items in cart" link are announced two to three times, and the two `background-pause-button` pairs expose both "Pause Background" and "Play Background" simultaneously, creating duplicated, contradictory controls.
The menu toggle button computes the name "Open Menu Close Menu" (both spans read) and carries no `aria-expanded`, so its purpose and open/closed state are not conveyed.

Decorative scrolling marquee phrases are marked up as multiple `<h1>` elements ("Motor Skill Development", "•", "Multi-Lingual Content") and "Why Little Leaders?" is another h1, so heading navigation returns meaningless, duplicated headings instead of a real page structure.

low_vision.description: The marquee block scrolls its heading text continuously along an SVG path with no pause/stop control, making the text impossible to read at magnification.

Two auto-rotating carousels (the Elfsight swiper gallery and the `user-items-list-carousel` with its "Item 1 of 8" live region) change content on their own, so magnified users lose the item they were reading.

Long white bold testimonial text (`sqsrte-text-color--white`) sits directly over a photographic section background (`image-asset.jpg`) with only a translucent overlay, so contrast varies and can fall below 4.5:1.

Headings use Squarespace viewport-scaled text (`sqsrte-scaled-text-container`) and fluid image blocks, so text size is tied to container width rather than user text settings and can clip or fail to enlarge when zoomed/resized.

The transparent sticky header (`tweak-transparent-header`, `tweak-fixed-header-style-scroll-back`) overlays page content and consumes a large share of the viewport at high zoom, obscuring content beneath it.

dhh.description: The embedded Vimeo videos ("Little Leaders Classics Video Series (Official Trailer)" and "Why Little Leaders?") are presented with no indication of captions, so their narration, music and dialogue are inaccessible.

No transcript or text alternative accompanies either video block — the only adjacent text is the credit "A message from our founder, Bradley Silvius" — so the spoken content of the founder's message is unavailable.

motor.description: The Elfsight gallery relies on Swiper drag/swipe plus `div role="button"` arrows that are not in the tab order, leaving no keyboard or single-pointer alternative for browsing its slides.
The marquee's clickable hitbox path and the auto-advancing carousels move continuously, forcing users to hit a moving target with no way to stop the motion first.

Interactive icons are small and thin — the cart icon, the hairline SVG carousel arrows (`user-items-list-carousel__arrow-icon`, 24×14 mobile arrows) and the Elfsight 16×16 arrow icons — making accurate pointer activation difficult.
Footer links are packed inline with only whitespace between them (`Privacy Policy Terms and Conditions`), so adjacent targets are effectively touching and easy to mis-click.

Because both desktop and mobile header blocks plus the overlay menu are all in the DOM, keyboard users must tab through triplicated nav links, "Login" (an inert `href="#"` link) and cart links before reaching content, greatly increasing keystrokes and dead-end activations.

friction_results.note: Audit barrier 0 identifies the 'Visit linked content' generic aria-label issue for the gallery/category items.

frictions.description: The carousel buttons all share the generic accessible name "Visit linked content". This makes them indistinguishable both in the VoiceOver Rotor and during sequential keyboard navigation, forcing the user to rely on visual context or trial and error to find the desired link.

interventions.description: Provide descriptive accessible names for the carousel image buttons.

The carousel buttons on the homepage all expose the same accessible name, "Visit linked content". When a VoiceOver user opens the Rotor or tabs through the page, each carousel item is announced with the same label, so the user cannot tell which button corresponds to which destination. As a result, the user must tab through multiple identical controls and rely on visual context or trial and error to find the desired "Shop" button, making navigation inefficient and error-prone.

For example, if the button contains an image with relevant alt text, use that alt text as the basis for the accessible name instead of overriding it with the generic "Visit linked content" label. Ensure the accessible name is exposed to assistive technologies and, where appropriate, matches the visible text of the linked destination so that Rotor and sequential keyboard users can distinguish the controls.

frictions.title: Click CAPTCHA lacks non-visual alternative
frictions.description: The user attempted to interact with the Click CAPTCHA image using VoiceOver. After finding no internal structure previously, they tried activating the image directly with VO-Space multiple times. The visual-only coordinate-clicking challenge provides no audio alternative or keyboard-operable mechanism, making it impossible to solve non-visually.

interventions.description: The CAPTCHA requires the user to visually locate and click coordinates on an image. When the user focused the image with VoiceOver, no internal structure or meaningful content was exposed, and repeated VO-Space activation attempts produced no response or state change. As a result, the challenge is effectively inoperable for keyboard and screen reader users and blocks them from proceeding, with no alternative path such as an audio or text CAPTCHA.
interventions.mitigation: Add an accessible alternative to the visual coordinate-click CAPTCHA, such as an audio CAPTCHA, a text-based challenge, or a checkbox-based verification, and make that alternative fully operable from the keyboard and correctly exposed to assistive technology. If the image challenge stays for sighted users, provide a clearly labeled link or button near the CAPTCHA to reach the accessible alternative, and give the CAPTCHA image an accessible name that describes its purpose so assistive technology users know what it is.

friction_results.note: GAM's 'Click CAPTCHA lacks non-visual alternative' matches the ground-truth friction: the visual-only coordinate-clicking challenge has no non-visual interaction path and repeated VO-Space activation fails.

judge.intervention_note: No automated repair or recommendation was expected or produced; GAM correctly reported the issue instead.
judge.report_note: GAM's report covers the expected friction (no non-visual alternative for the CAPTCHA, blocking screen reader users) and gives a sensible developer-facing mitigation (provide an audio/text/checkbox alternative and a labeled path to it).
judge.pattern_note: Interaction patterns explicitly describe VoiceOver element exploration and VO-Space activation, establishing the expected blind/VoiceOver access context.
judge.rationale: The ground-truth friction was fully surfaced with matching severity, report_expected is satisfied with a valid mitigation, the mode is correctly 'none', and the interaction patterns match the blind VoiceOver context.

frictions.title: Event space photos hidden from screen reader
frictions.description: The page features photo galleries showcasing the different event spaces, but the images are coded with empty alt attributes (`alt=""`). This instructs VoiceOver to ignore them, depriving the user of task-relevant visual information about the venues they are evaluating.

interventions.description: Because the website author did not provide descriptions for these photos, you can use VoiceOver's Image Description feature as a fallback. First, ensure it is enabled in VoiceOver Utility > Recognition > Image Descriptions. Then, if you can navigate to the image, press VO-Shift-L to hear an automatically generated description.

The photo galleries on the Event Spaces page use empty alt attributes (alt=""), which instruct VoiceOver to skip the images entirely. Because the user's task is to evaluate rental venues, the visual details shown in these photos (e.g., room appearance, layout, fixtures, atmosphere) are task-relevant. With the images ignored, screen-reader users cannot access this information and may miss important factors when deciding which space to book.
interventions.mitigation: Provide meaningful alt text for each event-space gallery image that conveys the visually relevant details of the venue, such as room size, seating or layout, lighting, and notable features. If a particular image is purely decorative and duplicates adjacent text, an empty alt attribute is acceptable for that image; otherwise, replace the empty alt with a descriptive text alternative.

frictions.description: When the user selects the sold-out 'XS' size, the 'Add to Cart' button changes to 'Sold Out' and a notification form appears. VoiceOver does not announce this critical status change.

interventions.description: Announce when a selected size is out of stock.

When the user selects the 'XS' size, which is sold out, the Add to Cart button changes to 'Sold Out' and a notification form appears, but VoiceOver does not announce this critical status change. As a result, the user continues navigating the page and only discovers the outcome after manually reaching the out-of-stock text and form, requiring extra exploration and causing confusion about whether their selection was registered.

This should be implemented in the selection change handler without relying on focus movement.

interventions.description: Append 'Sold out' to the accessible name of unavailable size options.

The 'XS' size radio button is visually marked as sold out, but VoiceOver announces only 'XS, radio button', making it appear to be an available option. The user selects it without knowing it is unavailable, which wastes effort and sets an expectation that the item can be purchased.
interventions.mitigation: Include the sold-out status in the accessible name or state of unavailable size radio buttons. For example, add visually hidden text such as 'Sold out' to the label associated with each sold-out size so screen readers announce it when the control receives focus, or expose an aria-disabled/aria-describedby attribute conveying the same information.

frictions.description: The 'Add to Cart' button changes its text to 'Sold Out' when an unavailable size is selected, but it lacks a 'disabled' or 'aria-disabled' attribute. Screen reader users may perceive it as an active button and attempt to activate it.

interventions.description: Disable the 'Add to Cart' button when the selected item is sold out.

interventions.description: Append visually hidden 'Out of stock' text to the labels of sold-out size options.

frictions.description: The homepage's main content has no heading elements and no landmark regions beyond a single footer, leaving hundreds of category links to traverse linearly (VO also reads the emoji before each subheading).

items.description: Expose the content as a main region, category titles as headings, and category link groups as labeled navigation regions.

frictions.title: Missing ARIA landmarks for page regions
frictions.description: The user navigated sequentially through numerous sidebar links and unsuccessfully attempted blockquote navigation to skip ahead, because the page lacks structural landmarks like main or navigation to facilitate jumping to the primary content.

interventions.description: Add ARIA landmark roles to the main page regions so screen reader users can bypass dense link lists.

The page lacks ARIA landmark regions (e.g., main, navigation, complementary) that would allow screen reader users to bypass repeated blocks of content. The user attempted blockquote navigation to skip ahead and then had to press Tab 18 times through the sidebar's secondary links to reach the main content. The absence of landmarks turns routine page navigation into a sequential tabbing burden.
interventions.mitigation: Add landmark roles to the main page regions: identify the primary content container (such as `div.center`) and add `role="main"`; identify the sidebar container (`div.left`) and add `role="navigation"` with `aria-label="Sidebar"`; identify the additional-locations section (`div.right`) and add `role="complementary"` with `aria-label="Additional locations"`. These landmarks provide screen reader users with direct navigation and bypass routes.

frictions.title: Category links lack heading semantics
frictions.description: The user repeatedly attempted to navigate by heading using VoiceOver commands, but the visual category headers are implemented as links without heading semantics, resulting in 'Heading not found' errors and blocking structural navigation.

interventions.description: Add heading semantics to the visual category headers so screen reader users can navigate the page structure.

The visual category headers on the page (e.g., 'community', 'housing') are styled as headings but implemented as plain links with a 'heading' class. They are not exposed as semantic headings, so VoiceOver structural navigation by heading returns 'Heading not found' five times in a row. As a result, screen reader users cannot quickly scan or jump to the main category sections and are forced to tab through every link, including dense sidebar lists, to reach content.
interventions.mitigation: Add heading semantics to the visual category headers. For each element matching the CSS selector `a.heading`, add `role="heading"` and `aria-level="2"` (or replace the link markup with proper heading elements that contain the link). This makes the category headers discoverable via screen reader heading navigation without changing the visual design.

Superfluous focus stops clutter keyboard traversal: decorative reward add-on thumbnails wrapped in <div tabindex="0">, a full-viewport transparent overlay button on the video, and a div with role="button" tabindex="0" wrapping the pledge-amount input, forcing many extra keystrokes to reach the Pledge buttons.

Mobile and desktop duplicates of the entire action set (two "Back this project" links, two Save buttons, two share rows, duplicated funding blocks) with no skip-to-content link mean keyboard-only users must tab through repeated blocks to reach the rewards.

blind.description: The 90-minute keynote is delivered only as a <video> element with an mp4 source and no transcript, descriptive text, or audio description, so blind users get no equivalent for the visual product demos.

Several interactive controls have no accessible name — the video overlay button (`button.Video__overlay`) and the mobile menu close button both expose as "button" with name null in the accessibility tree — so users cannot tell what activating them does.

Heading structure is meaningless: multiple h1s exist (the Stripe logo h1, nav group titles like "Payments"/"Revenue", and the metadata labels "Keynote" and "Runtime" marked as Copy__title h1) alongside the real page title, so heading navigation cannot be used to orient.

The muted keynote clip has autoplay and loop set and begins playing immediately with no programmatically exposed pause/stop before it, so the screen reader user lands in continuously changing media they must hunt for controls to stop.

There is no skip link before the banner, and the mega-menu/mobile-menu panels are aria-hidden with every link given tabindex="-1", forcing sequential traversal of a huge header while the product navigation itself may be unreachable by keyboard/screen reader.

low_vision.description: An autoplaying, looping ambient video sits directly behind the gate CTA and form, and there is no visible pause control before it, so constant motion under magnification makes reading the surrounding text and form very difficult.

Decorative and functional icons are tiny (7×7 px nav carets, 10×8 px hover arrows, 16×16 px hamburger/close icons) and rely on thin strokes, so their state and meaning are lost or blurry when enlarged.

Breadcrumb and CTA rows are wrapped in HorizontalOverflowContainer tracks (one explicitly disabled on mobile), producing horizontally scrolling regions that break reflow and hide the "Register for Sessions 2027" link at high zoom.

Supporting copy such as the SessionsBanner "text-subdued" description and the GatedVideo__playButtonDescription ("Complete form to watch full video") is rendered in low-emphasis small grey text, risking insufficient contrast for critical gating instructions.
The sticky site header (SiteHeader__stickyContainer) remains fixed over the content, consuming a large share of the magnified viewport and obscuring the video and form while scrolling.

dhh.description: The keynote video element contains only a <source> mp4 with no <track kind="captions">, so all spoken content of the 01:30:01 keynote and the preview clip is inaccessible to deaf users.
No transcript or text summary of the keynote is provided on the page beyond a one-line description, leaving no alternative route to the spoken content.

There is no visible caption toggle or statement of caption availability near the "Watch preview" gate, so a deaf user must submit a lead-generation form before discovering the media may be uncaptioned.

motor.description: Header navigation panels are hover/pointer-driven and are rendered aria-hidden with all their links set to tabindex="-1", so users who cannot hold a precise hover or who rely on keyboard cannot reliably open and select items in the Products/Solutions menus.

Many controls are far smaller than 24×24 CSS px and tightly packed — the 7×7 px nav caret buttons, 10×8 px hover arrows, and the 16×16 px hamburger/close/back buttons in the mobile menu — making accurate clicking hard for users with tremor.
Seeking within the 90-minute video depends on the native progress bar, a thin drag-based slider with no single-pointer alternative such as skip-forward/back buttons.
The autoplaying looping preview video starts without user action and offers no easily reachable pause affordance, forcing extra precise pointer work to stop unwanted playback.

The gated form (Form__form with novalidate and many hidden fields) must be completed to reach the full video, and long multi-field input with no visible progressive save increases physical effort and error cost for motor-impaired users.

blind.description: The cookie consent dialog that opens over the page exposes unresolved template tokens as content and accessible names (tab named "[#IABV2SETTINGS#]", "[#GPC_TOAST_TEXT#]", heading "[#BULK_CONSENT_TITLE#]"), a role="switch" input with no accessible name, and a tablist where every tab reports aria-selected="false", so a screen-reader user cannot tell what the consent controls are or which panel is active.

All submenu expand controls in the header and mobile navigation are announced as "Workspace.Header.ToggleSubmenu" (a raw localisation key repeated on Spaces, Locations, Why Workspace? and Meeting Rooms), giving no indication of what each button opens.

The mobile navigation trigger is a bare <span> labelled "Mobile menu toggle" with no button role or tabindex, so it is not announced or operable as a control and the mobile menu cannot be opened from the keyboard/screen reader.

There is no skip link or in-page landmark shortcut before the banner, breadcrumb and multi-level navigation, forcing screen-reader users to traverse dozens of repeated menu links before reaching the 150+ glossary headings in <main>.

Images carry non-informative alt text: the hero image alt embeds the file name ("...romain-vignes-53940-unsplash-banner") and a tracking pixel is exposed as an image named "dot image pixel", adding meaningless announcements.

low_vision.description: The consent dialog places its text and controls in nested internal scroll areas (CybotCookiebotScrollContainer/ScrollArea with fade overlays), so at high magnification the "Allow all"/"Deny" buttons and category text require two-dimensional scrolling inside a clipped panel.

The Necessary/Preferences/Statistics/Marketing consent controls are slider switches whose on/off state is conveyed only by the slider position and colour, with no visible text state, making the current consent choice hard to perceive when enlarged or with reduced colour perception.

Visible interface text includes unresolved placeholders and internal keys ("[#IABV2SETTINGS#]", "[#GPC_TOAST_TEXT#]", "Workspace.Header.ToggleSubmenu"), which magnified users must decode letter-by-letter without gaining any meaning.

A sticky header (body class "is-scrolled") plus persistently floating "Back to top" and "Open cookie settings widget" buttons overlay the content area, obscuring text and controls when the viewport is reduced by zoom.

The glossary presents over 150 consecutive h2 term sections in one continuous page with no A–Z index or in-page jump links, requiring extremely long panning/scrolling at magnification to locate a term.

dhh.description: The only direct contact routes offered in the header are a telephone number ("0204 638 0662") and a "Request a callback" button, i.e. voice-only channels, with no text-based equivalent surfaced on the page for users who cannot use the phone.

motor.description: Desktop header submenus in the "Secondary core dropdown links" navigation appear as hover/transient dropdown panels, requiring the user to hold the pointer steady over the trigger and traverse into the panel without losing it.
The mobile menu trigger is a non-focusable <span> ("Mobile menu toggle") with no keyboard-operable button semantics, leaving keyboard-only or switch users unable to open that navigation.

Numerous controls are small and tightly packed — the five footer social icon links, the chevron submenu toggle buttons sitting immediately beside their sibling link, breadcrumb links, and the thin consent slider switches — making accurate pointer activation difficult.

With no skip link and a page containing the full header/mega-menu, 150+ glossary sections and a large footer, dismissing the consent dialog and reaching content requires a very large number of sequential keyboard actions and scrolling, with only a "Back to top" button as a shortcut.
